title: AutoVoyage
tagline: AI agent plans and books full travel itineraries, paying per-query in HBAR via x402 on Hedera.
description:
Our AI travel agent plans and books full trip itineraries end-to-end, autonomously paying for real flight data over Hedera's x402 payment protocol. Instead of API keys or subscriptions, the agent pays per-query in native HBAR through a self-hosted x402 facilitator that verifies and settles each payment on Hedera testnet in real time.

The user authorizes once — setting a spending budget and approving a HIP-336 HBAR allowance in their HashPack wallet. From there, the agent searches and pays for flight (and stay/activity) data autonomously from the user's own account, with every payment checked against on-chain spending ceilings before it settles — non-custodial and revocable at any time.

Before booking, the agent requires an explicit human confirmation bound to the exact itinerary hash, preventing any bait-and-switch between what was quoted and what gets booked. Every payment, approval, booking, and refusal is written as a plaintext event to a public Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic, giving a fully auditable trail anyone can verify on HashScan — no black box, no trust required.

The paid flight-data supplier is a real, live x402 service (not a mock) with metered per-result pricing, and it also self-registers on an HCS-based agent registry with a signed identity claim, so other agents can discover it and verify who they're paying without a hardcoded endpoint.
how_its_made:
The stack is a monorepo: a Next.js frontend (the planner/agent), an Express-based supplier service (the paid flight-data API), and a self-hosted x402 facilitator, all wired for Hedera testnet.

Payments (x402 + HBAR): The supplier gates its search routes with HTTP 402 — each request returns a price, the agent signs an HBAR transfer, and the facilitator verifies + settles on-chain before the real data is returned. Pricing is metered per result (not a flat fee), using a quote cache keyed by a canonical hash of the query so the unpaid 402 price and the paid response always agree.

Autonomous, non-custodial payment: Rather than the agent holding user funds, we use Hedera's HIP-336 HBAR allowance. The user signs once in HashPack to grant a spending allowance; the agent then pays the supplier directly from the user's account using its own server-held key, with every payment checked against on-chain spending ceilings before settling. This took real HAPI-level probing to get right — Hedera requires the spender (our agent), not the fee-payer or facilitator, to own the transaction ID for an allowance-debited transfer, a rule that's undocumented for HBAR (only stated for NFTs in the protobufs) and had to be discovered empirically with test transactions.

Auditability (HCS): Every payment, human approval, booking, and refusal is written as a plaintext JSON event to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, readable live via Mirror Node — a public, tamper-evident audit trail with no local cache. The supplier also self-registers on a second HCS topic with a signed identity claim (Ed25519), so other agents can discover and verify it without a hardcoded URL or trusted middleman.

Booking safety: Before any booking executes, the agent re-derives a SHA-256 hash of the exact itinerary (flights, prices, passenger count) server-side and requires it to match a human-confirmed session — preventing a stale or swapped itinerary from being booked without consent.

The honest hack — flight data: Real flight-search APIs (Amadeus, Duffel, etc.) are paid and gated behind commercial contracts we couldn't get for a hackathon timeline, and scraping live fares isn't something we were willing to do. So the "supplier" is a real, live x402-gated service — the payment, pricing, and settlement are 100% real on-chain — but the flight inventory it serves is a curated dummy dataset rather than a live GDS feed. Every dollar (well, tinybar) spent buying that data is a genuine Hedera testnet transaction; the data itself is fixtures. We were explicit about this boundary throughout the build rather than dressing it up as real.
auto_summary: A monorepo travel-planning app uses Hedera-based x402 payments, HBAR allowances, and HCS audit logging to buy metered supplier data.
